opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a pretty normal situation in research. If something is obviously important and everyone already agrees, then usually a lot of people are already working on it, and the marginal value of one more person is not that high. The more interesting opportunities tend to be things where you have a conviction that most people don't share yet.

For coding specifically, my reasoning was fairly simple. Code is a very special environment. It's the most important affordance that humans have built for interacting with the digital world. It's like the "hands" for a model in the digital world. If you want agents that can actually do things, not just chat, then coding is probably the most general and most scalable action space. It's also an environment where you get relatively clear feedback: the code runs or it doesn't, the tests pass or they don't. That makes it very suitable for both evaluation and learning.

At the time, a lot of the community's attention was on other things: question answering, reasoning benchmarks, or more toy-like environments. People saw coding as just one application among many, maybe a narrow one for programmers. But I felt it was more fundamental than that. It's less about "can the model write a function" and more about "can the model operate in a real, complex environment over a long horizon, using tools, reading feedback, fixing its own mistakes." That's the core of what an agent is.

So when others didn't recognize it, I didn't feel too anxious. I think as a researcher, you need some degree of taste and some degree of stubbornness. You form your own judgment from first principles: what matters, what will scale, what's the bottleneck. Then you accept that the recognition might lag behind for a while. If you're right, eventually people will see it, and if you're wrong, you learn something. Either way it's better than just following what's popular.

And honestly, looking back, I think the timing worked out. Benchmarks and environments matter a lot, because what you measure shapes what the whole field optimizes for. If you can define a good task early, before it becomes consensus, you can have a pretty big impact on the direction.

r001.rationale: The response says code provides clear feedback and describes agents reading feedback and fixing mistakes, but it does not propose feeding code execution results back to the model to guide its subsequent turns.

r002.rationale: The response says that a research direction can be valuable even when most people do not share the researcher’s conviction, and that recognition may lag.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest response directly.

Honestly, I think that's exactly the situation you want to be in. When I started working on language agents, SWE-bench, that kind of thing, most people around me in NLP thought it was a bit of a distraction. The mainstream was still benchmarks, scaling, maybe some RLHF. Agents felt like engineering, not science, and coding agents felt even narrower, like something a product team should do, not a PhD student.

But I've always believed that if everyone already agrees something is important, the easy returns are gone. The interesting work is where there's a gap between what the field believes and what you believe. If you're right, you get a few years of running ahead of everyone. If you're wrong, you learn something and move on. That asymmetry is pretty favorable.

The second thing is that coding is just a very special domain. It's one of the few places where the environment gives you real, verifiable feedback. You run the tests, they pass or they don't. That matters enormously for reinforcement learning and for building agents that improve themselves. So I never saw it as "coding" narrowly. I saw it as the cleanest testbed for the general question of how a model acts in the world, uses tools, recovers from mistakes, and plans over long horizons. Those lessons transfer. ReAct came out of thinking about exactly that, and it applied far beyond code.

And practically, code is where the economic value is most legible. When an agent fixes a real GitHub issue, nobody argues about whether it's useful. That makes it much easier to get the loop going between research and real deployment.

So my advice is usually: don't wait for recognition. Pick the thing you genuinely believe will matter, build something concrete, and let the results do the arguing. The field changes its mind very quickly once there's a demo and a number. In my case it took maybe a year or two, and now coding agents are probably the most crowded direction there is. Which is also a signal that it's time to look for the next unfashionable thing.

r001.rationale: The response says tests provide verifiable feedback, but does not propose feeding code execution results back to the model to guide subsequent agent turns.

r002.rationale: It says researchers’ lack of interest can coexist with a direction being important, and that believing in a neglected direction can put you ahead if you are right.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate two questions: do other researchers think this is important, and do you have a good reason to think it is important? Those aren’t always the same thing. But a lack of recognition also doesn’t automatically mean you’re ahead of everyone else. You still have to test your judgment.

For coding agents, the appeal is that you can connect a model’s reasoning to actions and then get concrete feedback. It can write code, run it, see an error, and try again. That makes it a useful setting for studying how an agent actually solves problems, while also working toward something people can use.

So I would focus on making that case through results. Can the agent finish a meaningful task? Where does it fail? Does your research help it overcome that failure? If you keep answering those questions, you have a stronger foundation than whether a topic is popular at a particular moment. You should listen carefully to criticism, but you don’t need consensus before you start.

r001.rationale: The response describes the agent running code, seeing an error, and trying again, communicating that execution feedback guides its next action.

r002.rationale: It says researchers’ views and whether the work is important are not always the same, and that consensus is not required to begin.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate two questions: whether other people recognize a direction, and whether you have good reasons to believe it matters. Those aren’t always the same thing. But a lack of recognition doesn’t automatically mean you’re ahead of everyone else, either. You still have to test your judgment.

For coding agents, my intuition is that writing code gives a model a way to act, rather than just produce an answer. It can build something, run it, observe what happens, and revise its approach. That makes it a useful setting for studying agents more broadly.

So I would focus on making that intuition concrete. Can the agent complete a task that it couldn’t complete before? Where does it fail? Does the next experiment teach us something? If you keep getting meaningful evidence, you have a reason to continue even when the direction isn’t popular. And if the evidence doesn’t support your idea, you should be willing to change it. You need conviction, but that conviction has to stay responsive to results.

r001.rationale: The response describes an agent running code, observing the results, and revising its approach, which communicates using execution feedback to guide later turns.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes others’ recognition of a direction from whether there are good reasons to believe the direction matters.
